title: EU AI Act Art 50(2) — Third-Party Verification Failure Modes (Council of AI, 2026-10-07)
context: 2026-10-07 EAT cycle — this seed examines the failure modes of Art 50(2) marking in practice: where deployers and platforms fail to meet the third-party verifiability requirement, and how the Council of AI measurement framework addresses each failure mode. Complements the 2026-10-06 seed on marking as measurement surface.
body: EU AI Act Article 50(2) requires that synthetic-content markings be detectable by third parties using 'appropriate technical instruments.' In practice, this requirement breaks in three predictable ways — and the Council of AI measurement framework is designed to detect each. Failure mode 1: proprietary-only marking. A platform embeds a watermark that is only detectable by the platform's own detection API. The third party cannot verify the marking without calling the deployer's endpoint — which means the marking is not independently verifiable, and the deployer has created a lock-in dependency disguised as compliance. The Council of AI measurement board tests for this by running marking-detection through at least three independent parsers (the platform's own, an open-source reference implementation, and a standards-body tool). If the marking is only detectable by one of the three, the axis score for marking-robustness drops to zero on that observation. Failure mode 2: marking fragility under adversarial modification. A synthetic image carries a C2PA manifest, but a trivial crop-and-re-encode destroys the manifest while leaving the image visually identical. The marking was present but not robust. The Council of AI tests marking-robustness by applying a standardised adversarial transformation set (crop, resize, re-encode at quality 75, screenshot-and-recapture) and checking whether the marking survives each transformation. This is a measurement, not a claim — the signed capsule records exactly which transformations destroyed the marking and which preserved it. Failure mode 3: marking but no provenance chain. A system applies a watermark but cannot produce a signed record of when the marking was applied, which model generated the content, or what the input prompt was. The marking exists, but the provenance chain is broken. The Council of AI's verified measurement credential addresses this by binding the marking observation to a board manifest that includes model identifier, generation timestamp, and measurement-capsule hash. The credential does not claim the content is safe — it claims that the marking was measured, that the provenance chain is intact, and that the record is signed. For deployers preparing for Art 50(2) enforcement (August 2025 application for transparency obligations, phased rollout for high-risk systems), the operational question is not 'do we have a watermark?' but 'can a third party verify our watermark without trusting our platform?' If the answer is no, the marking is decoration, not compliance. The Council of AI framework provides the measurement evidence to close that gap — not by claiming isolation from marking failures, but by continuously monitoring and signing the observation that marking is present, robust, and provenance-linked. This is monitored containment of the marking obligation, not provable isolation from marking failure.
